content:
The **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** is a UK statute enacted during the final months of the Labour government (May–October 2010), following the May 2010 general election that resulted in a Conservative–Liberal Democrat coalition. It is important to clarify a common misconception: **there is no UK Finance (No. 2) Act 2010**.

✅ **Correct fact**:  
The UK Parliament passed the **Finance Act 2010** on **8 April 2010**, receiving Royal Assent on that date.  
There was **no separate "Finance (No. 2) Act 2010"**—the numbering convention “(No. 2)” was *not* used for 2010.

🔍 Why the confusion?
- The UK has occasionally passed *two* Finance Acts in a single calendar year — typically when a second budget occurs (e.g., after a change of government or an emergency fiscal statement). In such cases, the second is titled *Finance (No. 2) Act [Year]*.
- Notable examples:
  - **Finance (No. 2) Act 1997** (following Brown’s first budget as Chancellor).
  - **Finance (No. 2) Act 2005** (after the 2005 pre-election budget).
  - **Finance (No. 2) Act 2015** (following the July 2015 Budget after the Conservative majority win).
- However, **2010 did not have a second budget or a Finance (No. 2) Act**.

📋 What *did* happen in 2010:
- **Finance Act 2010** (c. 13) was enacted on **8 April 2010**, giving legal effect to the **March 2010 Budget** delivered by Alistair Darling (Chancellor under Gordon Brown).
- Key provisions included:
  - Increase in the main rate of corporation tax from 28% to 29% (effective from 1 April 2011 — later reversed by the incoming coalition).
  - Introduction of the **Bank Payroll Tax**, a one-off 50% tax on bonuses over £25,000 paid by banks between 9 December 2009 and 5 April 2010.
  - Adjustments to capital gains tax (e.g., clarification on entrepreneurs’ relief, changes to the annual exempt amount).
  - Measures to tackle tax avoidance (e.g., strengthening anti-avoidance rules for dual-resident companies and loan relationships).
  - Amendments to inheritance tax rules, including changes to the treatment of certain trusts.
- The Act received Royal Assent before the general election (6 May 2010) and entered into force as scheduled — even though the coalition government that took office in May 2010 subsequently announced policy reversals (e.g., scrapping the planned corporation tax rise in the 2010 Emergency Budget).

⚠️ Post-election developments:
- On **22 June 2010**, the new coalition government delivered an **Emergency Budget**, implemented via the **Finance Act 2010 (No. 2)**?  
❌ No — it was implemented via the **Finance Act 2010 (c. 13)** *as amended*?  
❌ Also incorrect.  
✅ In fact: The Emergency Budget’s measures were enacted through the **Finance Act 2010** *as originally passed* — **no second Act was required or passed in 2010**.  
Instead, the coalition used:
- **Commencement orders** and **regulations** (e.g., under existing enabling powers) for some measures,
- And crucially, the **Finance Act 2011**, which implemented the bulk of the 2010 Emergency Budget’s tax changes (e.g., the 50p top rate of income tax, VAT rise to 20%, corporation tax reductions).

✔️ Final clarification:
- **No Finance (No. 2) Act was passed in 2010.**  
- The only Finance Act for that year is the **Finance Act 2010 (c. 13)**.  
- The next Finance (No. 2) Act was **Finance (No. 2) Act 2015**, following George Osborne’s July 2015 Budget.

📚 Sources:
- UK Legislation website: [legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/13](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/13)
- House of Commons Library Standard Note SN/SG/5447 (Historical list of Finance Acts)
- HMRC’s archived budget documents (2010 Budget, Emergency Budget 2010)
